newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ deputy PM Peters admits ATN furore is damaging.
newsitem.headline: NZ deputy PM Peters admits ATN furore is damaging.

text.p: New Zealand's Deputy Prime Minster Winston Peters on Thursday admitted press coverage of mispending by an MP in his New Zealand First party was damaging the reputation of his party and the coalition government.

"I have got no doubt what the public perception is. It is hurting me, it is hurting my party, it is hurting the coalition," the NZ First leader told a press conference called to respond to allegations against Maori MP Tukoroirangi Morgan.
Peters described the allegations as baseless.
"I will not stand by and watch a colleague of mine being maltreated without any evidence," Peters told reporters.

Asked if he expected an ongoing investigation by the Serious Fraud Office (SFO) into Morgan and the formerly state-funded Aotearoa Television Network (ATN) to clear Morgan, Peters said, "I don't know, but I am happy to wait."
Opposition parties have called for Morgan to resign over the affair.
The centre-right coalition of nationalist New Zealand First and the conservative National Party has 61 seats in the 120 seat parliament.
If Morgan resigned a by-election could remove that majority.
But the single United Party MP and the eight members of free-market Act New Zealand would likely support the current administration, although they may not join the coalition.

Media reports have suggested Morgan spent money from pilot Maori language television broadcaster ATN to buy expensive clothes, including an NZ$89 pair of underpants, only weeks before he became an MP in October 1996.
Recent coverage has concentrated on how Morgan, a former director and presenter at ATN, may have continued financial links with the station after resigning his posts.
Morgan has said he had approval for the alleged spending, but the station has disputed this.
In February Cabinet approved extra funding for the station, but this was revoked after departmental reports questioned financial controls at ATN.
The station is still broadcasting using volunteers.
Prime Minister Jim Bolger said on Thursday he would not be commenting until the SFO had completed its report, which he expected would be completed in three to four weeks.
Bolger, Peters and Maori Affairs Minister Tau Henare -- Morgan's brother-in-law -- faced a barrage of questions about the affair in Parliament during the day.
